scenarios.title: Well Above Average
scenarios.axis: CU 02 resolving toward the school's instruments failing in a FLATTERING direction — every measure it owns reads high and reads wrong — crossed with CU 03 resolving toward the credential holding value everywhere except where the school issues it, because the people who hire and admit stopped trusting school-issued marks and built their own

based_on.title: Can a school still know what is true about its own students?
based_on.pole: Instruments wrong, and wrong upward. The gradebook, the survey, the portfolio all read well; the error is invisible because nothing it produces looks like a problem.

based_on.title: Does the academic credential hold its economic value, or does the market reprice it?
based_on.pole: Holds — but issued elsewhere. Universities and employers kept the idea of a credential and took over its manufacture, because a mark a school gives its own student stopped being evidence.

scenarios.premise: Nobody at Mount Vernon cheated and nothing broke. Coursework grades drifted up through the early 2030s the way they had for thirty years, and the school could point to real work behind every one of them. What changed was outside: the 2029 replication of the Hong Kong cohort study established that assisted coursework performance and unassisted capability come apart over about two years, and that the gap is widest among the strongest students. By 2032 the four universities Mount Vernon sends most students to had stopped reading transcripts as evidence and started running their own two-hour unassisted sittings. Employers followed. The school still issues a diploma. Everyone still accepts it — as a statement of attendance and character, which is what it now is.

personas.name: Aditi, 17
personas.vignette: She has a 3.9 and she sat the university panel in March and came out shaken. Nothing on it was unfair. It was just that every question kept going until she was somewhere she could not get to alone, and she had never been to that edge before, because at school the work always resolved. She is not angry at anyone. She has started doing one problem a week with the wifi off, in a notebook, badly, and she has not told her teachers because she cannot work out whether it would sound like an insult.

personas.name: Mr. Vance, 16 years in
personas.vignette: He knows the number is soft. He has known since about 2031, when a student who wrote beautifully for him could not reconstruct the argument out loud two days later. He raised it. The response was reasonable and he agreed with it at the time: we do not accuse students on a hunch. So the grade stands, the grade is honest by the school's own rules, and the rules produce a number he no longer believes. What he cannot say at parent evening is that his A means something narrower than it used to, because the sentence has no ending that does not sound like he is confessing to something.

personas.name: Marcus
personas.vignette: He is paying $58,000 for an institution whose central artefact the market has quietly stopped reading. He is not sure that is the school's fault, and he notices he wants it to be. His daughter is thriving by every measure the school produces and was rattled by the first measure it did not produce, and he has been turning over a thought he does not like: that he has spent eleven years buying a signal, and that the signal was always the point, and that he would still be here if it were only the education.

personas.name: Dr. Ellis, Head of School
personas.vignette: She could institute unassisted sittings tomorrow. She has modelled it: the school's average would fall, visibly, in the first year, into a market where three competitor schools have not done it and are advertising their averages. The families who would applaud the honesty are not the families who fill the class. What she keeps returning to is that the four universities are now doing for free — and better — the thing the school exists to certify, and that the honest response is not to compete with them but to stop pretending the transcript is the product. She has not found a way to say that in a viewbook.

scenarios.tension: An instrument that fails downward gets fixed, because the failure announces itself. This one failed upward. Every number the school produced went on looking healthy while the thing underneath thinned out, and by the time anyone could prove it, the proof was being generated somewhere else by people with no stake in being gentle. So the school lost its evidentiary authority without a scandal, a ruling, or a single dishonest act — just a slow divergence between what it measured and what was there. And the correction is available, cheap and immediately punishing: any school can start testing unassisted, and the first one to do it posts worse numbers than the schools that don't. Honesty is a real option and it is priced.
provocations: Take one course. What would our grade distribution look like if half the assessment were unassisted and in the room? Are we willing to find out privately before someone finds out publicly?
Our graduates are now assessed by people who owe us nothing. Do we know how they do — and if we don't collect that, is it because it's hard or because we'd rather not?
If the transcript is no longer what the market reads, what is the product we are charging $58,000 for? Say it in one sentence that a parent would recognise as true.

scenarios.title: The Instrument
scenarios.axis: CU 02 resolving toward evidence rebuilt — the school narrows to the few instruments it directly controls, chiefly work performed under observed conditions — crossed with CU 05 resolving toward the campus as essential, but for an unsentimental reason: it is the only place where a claim about a student can be generated under known conditions

based_on.title: Can a school still know what is true about its own students?
based_on.pole: Evidence rebuilt — fewer instruments, directly controlled, with known error bars. What was not observed is not asserted.

based_on.title: Does the physical campus become more essential — or a stranded asset?
based_on.pole: Essential — as a measurement facility. Everything else can happen anywhere; only here can you say under what conditions it happened.

scenarios.premise: Mount Vernon's 2036 argument is the strongest one it has ever had, and the least romantic. Every remote claim about a student — the take-home task, the survey, the vendor's engagement score, the recommendation written from a rubric bank — degraded past the point of use in the early 2030s. What survived was the room: work done in a place, watched by an adult who knows the discipline, on a day everyone can name. The school sells conditions. It works. Applications are up. And because a conditioned square foot now costs what it costs — the utility line tripled between 2028 and 2034 — the school has had to ask, seriously, of every space on the property: what evidence does this room produce? The rooms that answered are thriving. The quad did not answer.

personas.name: Priya, 16
personas.vignette: She likes the studio blocks; three hours, one problem, somebody watching who can tell when she is bluffing. She is better than she was and she knows it, which is not nothing. What she notices is that the day has no seams. Free periods were consolidated into a supervised commons in 2033 for reasons she has heard explained and found reasonable. She and her friends have started eating lunch in the stairwell by the loading dock because it is the only place on campus with no camera and no adult, and she is aware that this is the single most important thing about it, and she is not sure whether that is a fact about her or about the building.

personas.name: Mr. Adeyemi, 12 years in
personas.vignette: He believes in the model. He watched the old evidence base rot — the vendor dashboards, the surveys nobody could stand behind — and what replaced it is a discipline he respects: you saw it or you don't say it. What he cannot argue for, in the language the model runs on, is the twenty minutes after class when a kid lingers by the door and eventually says the thing. That produced no artefact and no observation record and it is where he has done most of his actual work for twelve years. When the schedule was tightened to protect observed hours, those twenty minutes were the slack that got taken. Nobody removed them. They just were not defended by anything.

personas.name: Ingrid
personas.vignette: She chose this school specifically for the rigour of what it will assert. Her son's reports say less than her own school reports did and every sentence in them is true, which after a decade of confident nonsense she finds close to moving. Her hesitation is smaller and she keeps setting it down and picking it up: she has read four reports now and could not tell you from any of them whether her son is happy. She raised it once. The answer was honest — we don't have an instrument for that, and we stopped guessing. She respects the answer. She wanted a different one.

personas.name: Dr. Ellis, Head of School
personas.vignette: She built this and it saved the place. She can also read the facilities model, which now scores rooms by observed contact hours per conditioned square foot, and she knows what that metric does over ten years to a quad, a chapel, a corridor wide enough to stop in. She has protected the quad twice, both times on her own authority, both times without a number. She has started to wonder what happens when the head after her inherits the model and not the instinct — because the model is written down and the instinct is not, and she has spent four years insisting that what is not written down cannot be asserted.

scenarios.tension: The school did the honest thing. It stopped claiming what it could not evidence, narrowed to the instruments it controls, and became more truthful than it has ever been — and the truthfulness gave the building its purpose back, because conditions can only be guaranteed in a place. But an institution that only asserts what it observes will, over time, only fund what it observes, and the parts of a school that formed people were never observations: the lingering at the door, the unsupervised lunch, the walk across a quad that produces nothing. Those didn't lose an argument. They were never in the argument, because the reform that rescued the school's honesty was also a rule about what counts as a reason. The stairwell by the loading dock is the last place on campus that generates no evidence, which is precisely why the students go there.
provocations: Name three things this school does that produce no evidence and that we would defend anyway. Who currently has the authority to defend them, and what happens when that person leaves?
If we scored every room by what it lets us assert about a student, which spaces would fail — and is that a finding about those spaces or about the score?

We have an instrument for what a student can do. What would an honest, small, defensible instrument for how a student is look like — and is 'we stopped guessing' an answer we are comfortable giving a parent for ten more years?

scenarios.title: The Dose
scenarios.axis: CU 01 resolving toward the inverted U being real — metered AI use helps, unmetered use erodes, and the curve is published and replicated — crossed with CU 04 resolving toward liability as governor, so that a known dose-response curve converts into a documented duty and the pedagogy becomes a compliance regime

based_on.title: Does routine AI use build human capability or quietly dissolve it?
based_on.pole: Neither pole — a dose curve. Once or twice a week beats both abstinence and daily use, and by 2031 the finding has survived replication in four countries.

based_on.title: Does institutional liability become the real governor of what schools may do?
based_on.pole: Liability as governor — the moment a dose-response curve is public and replicated, exceeding it is a documented failure to act, and the curve becomes an enforceable standard of care.

scenarios.premise: The PISA finding held. Metered use beat both extremes, the effect replicated, and by 2030 nobody serious argued about it. What nobody predicted was the second step: in 2032 a settled negligence claim in Ohio turned the curve into a standard of care, and every carrier writing educational liability wrote it into the renewal. Mount Vernon now runs a Managed Cognitive Load policy. Every student has a weekly AI allocation — three sessions, logged at the identity layer, exportable on request. The school is compliant, the audit is clean, and the policy is, as far as anyone can tell from the data, pedagogically correct. It is also the single most surveilled thing that happens in the building, and it is the part of school that students now describe, without much prompting, as the part that is being done to them.

personas.name: Marisol, 16
personas.vignette: She uses two of her three sessions on Monday because that is when the physics set is due, and then spends Thursday stuck on something she could have unstuck in four minutes. She has learned that the correct move is to be stuck on Monday, which is a scheduling skill, not a thinking one. Her friend Tobi uses a family account at home — not banned, not logged, not anything — and everyone knows. Marisol is not angry about Tobi. She is bothered by something smaller and harder to say: the school built a rule around the best evidence available and the rule taught her to game a counter, and she cannot tell whether the adults know that or have decided not to.

personas.name: Ms. Ibarra, 9 years in
personas.vignette: She believes the curve. She has read the four replications and she has watched the unmetered kids in 2029 go glassy and fluent and thin. What she cannot get past is that the intervention she believes in arrives to her students as a quota with a log, so the message they receive is not this is how thinking works, it is we are counting. She used to say think about when you actually need it and now she says you have one left. She is aware that she has been converted from a teacher of judgment into an administrator of an allowance, and that the conversion happened because the alternative was legally indefensible, not because anyone thought it was better.

personas.name: Renée
personas.vignette: She is a compliance officer at a regional bank and she recognises this policy immediately, in her bones: it is a control designed to be evidenced, not a practice designed to work. It will hold up beautifully in an audit. She also knows her daughter does most of her real thinking at the kitchen table at 9pm on a household account nobody counts, which means the school's log is a record of a fraction of the behaviour it claims to govern. She has not raised this at a parent evening. She has worked out that if she does, the likely response is to extend the logging into her house, and she would rather have the incoherence than that.

personas.name: Dr. Ellis, Head of School
personas.vignette: She wrote the policy and she can defend every line of it, including the parts she dislikes. The carrier's language was not negotiable; the standard of care exists whether or not she agrees with how it was made. What keeps her up is narrower than the surveillance question. It is that the school's most important pedagogical commitment is now indistinguishable, from the inside, from a compliance obligation — and that in six years, when the evidence moves and the curve shifts, the thing she will have to change is not a practice but a policy, with counsel in the room, and it will take two years instead of a term.

scenarios.tension: For once the evidence was good and the school followed it. That is the problem. A dose-response curve is a finding about judgment — when a tool helps and when it hollows you out — and the only way an institution can act on a finding at scale, under a duty of care, is to convert it into a countable rule. So the school gets the right answer and loses the thing the right answer was about: the students learn to schedule around a quota rather than notice when they are reaching for help too early, and the teacher who understood the curve is now enforcing it. Nobody defected from good practice. Good practice was metabolised into compliance by an institution that had no other way to hold it, and the strongest evidence base in the field turned out to be the mechanism by which pedagogy stopped being a professional judgment.
provocations: Name a pedagogical commitment we currently hold that would become a countable rule the moment it was strong enough to be legally expected of us. Would we still want it?
Our AI policy governs what happens on our network. What fraction of our students' actual AI use does that cover, and what does the gap mean for every claim we make about it?
If the evidence base moved next year, how long would it take us to change practice — and is that number a fact about our pedagogy or about our counsel?

scenarios.title: Discoverable
scenarios.axis: CU 04 resolving toward liability as governor — what a school records is decided by counsel, not by pedagogy — crossed with CU 03 resolving toward the credential HOLDING its value, for the unexpected reason that the transcript is the one document about a child that has been hardened against legal challenge

based_on.title: Does institutional liability become the real governor of what schools may do?
based_on.pole: Liability as governor — documented duty sets the boundary of practice; retention schedules and counsel decide what teachers write down about children.

based_on.title: Does the academic credential hold its economic value, or does the market reprice it?
based_on.pole: Holds — and hardens. After a decade in which every other claim about a student became contestable, the audited, timestamped, appealable transcript survives as the only assertion an institution will stand behind.

scenarios.premise: By 2035 the transcript is a legal instrument. Three waves did it: the negligence-per-se line that made a missed statutory duty actionable on its face, the discovery orders that pulled a decade of advisory notes into two separate suits, and the carrier language that now prices pastoral-record practice directly. Mount Vernon's response was orderly and, everyone agrees, correct. Advisory observations are retained 180 days. Narrative comments were retired in 2031 in favour of a rubric bank of 340 approved statements. The transcript itself, by contrast, got better: every grade carries an evidence link, an appeal window and a timestamp, and it is the one document about a child the school has been willing to defend under oath. Universities and employers noticed. The credential is worth more than it was in 2026 — because it is now the only part of the record that means anything.

personas.name: Theo, 17
personas.vignette: He had a bad year in Year 10 — his father was ill, and he stopped turning things in. Two teachers noticed and one of them, Mr. Reyes, more or less carried him through it. None of that is anywhere. The grades are, permanently, with evidence links. When he asked Mr. Reyes for a recommendation, he got a form: attendance, course rigour, three rubric statements from the approved bank. It was accurate. Theo read it four times looking for the year in it and eventually understood that the school's memory of him and his own memory of the school are two different documents, and only one of them is admissible.

personas.name: Mr. Reyes, 21 years in
personas.vignette: He still notices everything. He has simply stopped writing it down, and he did not decide this — it happened over four years of small, reasonable trainings. Say it in the room, not in the system. He is aware that the thing that made him good at this job is now the thing he practices off the record, and that when he retires in six years it leaves with him, because nothing he knew about a student was ever stored anywhere. He keeps a paper notebook in his bag. He knows what it is. He keeps it anyway.

personas.name: Devon
personas.vignette: He asked for his daughter's file after a placement decision he disagreed with, and he got it in eleven days, complete, beautifully organised, and it told him nothing. Grades with evidence links. Three rubric statements. No trace of the two years of conversations he had had with her teachers, all of which he remembers as substantive. His complaint has nowhere to go — the file is not incomplete, it is exactly what the retention policy says it should be. He has begun to suspect that the school's transparency and the school's opacity are the same policy, and that he preferred the version where he had to ask a person.

personas.name: Dr. Ellis, Head of School
personas.vignette: Her transcript is the best in the region and she is proud of it; the audit trail took four years and it is the reason three universities now take her school's grades at face value. She also signed the 180-day retention schedule, and she can trace the line from that signature to the fact that no adult in this building can now write a sentence about a child that will outlive a semester. Counsel calls it a clean posture. Her development office calls it a problem, because alumni give to people who remembered them. She has asked twice for a legal opinion on a protected pastoral record. Both times the answer was that anything you create is discoverable, and the only safe document is the one you never wrote.

scenarios.tension: The school got exactly what the decade demanded: a credential that holds because it can survive a challenge. But a record hardens by shedding everything that cannot be defended, and what could not be defended was the part that knew the child — the uncertain observation, the early worry, the note that says something is different this term. So the institution ends up with an unimpeachable account of a student's performance and no account at all of their formation, and it cannot fix this by writing more, because the writing is the exposure. The credential kept its value by becoming the only thing the school is willing to say. Nobody is doing anything wrong. Every clause is prudent. And a graduate now leaves with a document that would win in court and could not tell you who they were.
provocations: What do we currently record about a student that would survive a subpoena, and what do we record that we would rather not have to explain? Which of those two is the one we would want a parent to read?
Our retention schedule was written by counsel. Who in this school is responsible for arguing the cost side of it, and have we ever asked them to put a number on what a shorter memory costs us?
If the transcript is the only artefact anyone outside trusts, are we improving it because it is true or because it is defensible — and would we be able to tell the difference?

scenarios.title: Full House
scenarios.axis: CU 03 resolving toward the credential repriced by a labour market hiring in low-prestige sectors — crossed with CU 05 resolving toward the campus filling up, but from other schools' failures rather than its own draw

based_on.title: Does the academic credential hold its economic value, or does the market reprice it?
based_on.pole: Repriced — hiring concentrates in sectors school advising treats as fallbacks, while the knowledge-work destination schools sell keeps contracting.

based_on.title: Does the physical campus become more essential — or a stranded asset?
based_on.pole: Essential by default — public consolidation pushes families out of closing districts, and independent seats fill without the school having done anything to earn it.

scenarios.premise: Mount Vernon has a waitlist for the first time in fifteen years, and Dr. Ellis knows exactly why. Atlanta's public districts have closed forty-one schools since 2029 — the savings never materialised, the enrolment losses did — and each closure sends a wave of families who never intended to leave the system. The school is at 104% capacity. Sixty percent of its parents describe themselves as working class, including the ones earning $280,000. And the pathway the school sells, the four-year degree into knowledge work, is the one the labour market has spent five years quietly repricing downward while hiring in construction, care, food and skilled trades.

personas.name: Reuben, 16
personas.vignette: He arrived in Year 9 when his middle school closed, on 70% aid, and he is doing well. His uncle is a controls technician on data-centre builds clearing $190,000 and has offered to get him into the apprenticeship at eighteen. Reuben's advisor is supportive in the careful way adults are when they are worried about you. He can't tell whether the school is offering him a future or an argument, and he has noticed that the students whose parents went to college are the ones being told to keep their options open.

personas.name: Ms. Duarte, 13 years in
personas.vignette: Her classes have gone from eighteen to twenty-four, and a third of each section arrived mid-year from a closure. They are good kids carrying an interrupted transcript and a sense that school is something that happens to them. She is teaching more students, less well, to a curriculum aimed at a destination the Bureau of Labor Statistics stopped growing years ago. Nobody has asked her to change anything. Enrolment is up; from the board's angle, the year is a success.

personas.name: Yolanda
personas.vignette: She earns $310,000 as a hospital administrator and calls herself working class without irony — her father laid pipe, and she has decided that is what she is. She wants her son at a school with people like her, which now means something she could not define under oath. When the tuition letter came with a 6% increase, she felt the way she would have at twenty-five: squeezed, a little insulted. She gave to the annual fund anyway. She would not describe herself as wealthy to anyone, including herself.

personas.name: Dr. Ellis, Head of School
personas.vignette: Every metric she reports is up. The waitlist is real, aid applications are up 40%, and the discount rate is at 31% and climbing. She is filling classrooms with families displaced by other institutions' collapse, on a value proposition — the college pathway — that her own scan data says is weakening. She could say this out loud at the October board meeting. She has drafted it. The draft's problem is that it describes the school's best year in a decade as a form of drift, and she cannot find a version that does not sound ungrateful.

scenarios.tension: The school is succeeding and the success is not its own. Seats fill because neighbouring institutions are failing, not because the promise got more true — and the promise itself, a degree pathway into knowledge work, is the thing the labour market has been quietly discounting while it hires in the sectors this school's advising treats as consolation. Meanwhile the families arriving no longer describe themselves as the class the school is priced for, which makes every tuition conversation feel like a betrayal to people who are, by any measure but their own, affluent. Nothing here is a crisis. That is the difficulty: a full house is the least likely condition under which anyone reopens the question of what the house is for.
provocations: What share of our enrolment growth over the last three years came from families displaced by a school closure rather than families who chose us — and do we track the difference?
Our advising ranks pathways by prestige. If we ranked them by demonstrated local hiring, what would change, and who would object?
Our parent body increasingly does not identify as affluent. Does our tuition, aid and philanthropy messaging speak to the families we have, or the ones we think we have?

scenarios.title: The Offer
scenarios.axis: CU 01 resolving toward a hard capability ceiling — agents optimise but decay over long horizons, so verification becomes the scarce human skill — crossed with CU 03 resolving toward the credential being repriced by algorithmic direct admission

based_on.title: Does routine AI use build human capability or quietly dissolve it?
based_on.pole: Structural ceiling — agent reliability decays per step, so long-horizon judgment and checkpointed verification stay human and become the scarce good.

based_on.title: Does the academic credential hold its economic value, or does the market reprice it?
based_on.pole: Repriced by algorithm — admission arrives unbidden from a transcript match, and the essay, the recommendation and the pitch stop signalling anything.

scenarios.premise: By 2033 most students do not apply to college; they are matched to it. A transcript and a twenty-minute profile go into a state portal in September of senior year and offers come back in three weeks — no essays, no recommendations, no interview. It works, it is fairer than what it replaced, and the sector is calmer for it. Meanwhile employers have settled on the opposite skill: agents handle any bounded task and fail predictably past a dozen steps, so what a firm hires for is the person who notices, at step nine, that the machine is confidently wrong. Mount Vernon's students are admitted on a number and employed on a disposition, and the school has not found a way to teach toward both at once.

personas.name: Callum, 17
personas.vignette: He got four offers on 21 September without writing anything, which his parents found miraculous and he found deflating in a way he keeps to himself. The offers read his GPA, not the eleven months he spent on the water-quality project where the model kept insisting the sensor drift was seasonal and he proved it was a loose fitting. That is the part he is proud of. There is no field on the portal for it, and the first person who has asked him about it is a hiring manager at an internship interview, which felt like being seen for the first time.

personas.name: Ms. Okafor, 15 years in
personas.vignette: She teaches the verification seminar — students run agents on real problems and are graded on where they stopped and why. It is the best course she has built and the hardest to explain at parent evening, because it produces no artefact and its whole content is judgment exercised at a moment of doubt. Half her energy now goes to the transcript, because the transcript is what the portal reads, and she is aware that she is spending her time on the measure and her conviction on the thing the measure cannot see.

personas.name: Nia
personas.vignette: Her daughter has offers from two good universities and Nia has not been able to shake a specific unease: nobody at either institution has any idea who her daughter is. The match is honest and blind and that is the point — it was built to stop families like the ones she competed against from buying advantage. She got what she asked for. What she did not anticipate was that a system fair enough to ignore your money is also a system indifferent to your child, and she cannot work out whether she is describing a flaw or just grief.

personas.name: Dr. Ellis, Head of School
personas.vignette: Her admissions outcomes have never looked better and her enrolment inquiries are up, both driven by a number the portal reads off a transcript she controls. She also knows the school's real distinctive work — the seminars, the long projects, the verification habits — is invisible to that number and expensive to run. The rational move is to optimise the transcript and quietly thin the rest. She has not done it. She has also not stopped the two department heads who, without being told to, have already begun.

scenarios.tension: Two good things arrived together and pull opposite ways. Admission became fair by becoming blind, which stripped out the essay, the recommendation and the story — the machinery of advantage, yes, and also the only channel through which a school's actual formative work reached the institutions judging it. Meanwhile the labour market started paying for exactly what that machinery used to carry: judgment, doubt, the instinct to stop. So the school is measured on a number that cannot see its best work, and rewarded in a market that cannot see its number, and every efficient response to the first makes it worse at the second.
provocations: If a transcript is the only thing an admissions algorithm reads, what does our grading policy now signal — and did we design it for that job?
Our most distinctive work is the least legible to the systems that judge our students. Do we defend it on principle, find a way to make it legible, or stop pretending it drives outcomes?
Who at this school would notice if departments quietly began optimising for the transcript, and what would we do about it?

scenarios.title: The Quiet Campus
scenarios.axis: CU 04 resolving toward liability as governor — insurability and verdict exposure set what a building may be used for — crossed with CU 05 resolving toward the campus as essential place, marketed as community while operated as a controlled asset

based_on.title: Does institutional liability become the real governor of what schools may do?
based_on.pole: Liability as governor — the insurance renewal and the verdict environment, not the mission statement, decide what happens on the property.

based_on.title: Does the physical campus become more essential — or a stranded asset?
based_on.pole: Essential place — the school's whole value proposition is that it is where community physically happens.

scenarios.premise: Mount Vernon's 2034 case for itself is community: in a dispersed, virtualised, low-trust decade, this is where people are actually together. The viewbook says so on page two. The operations are the mirror image. After convective-storm losses reset the roof and canopy schedule, and after the verdict environment widened to reach any institution a jury reads as having known and not acted, the carrier's renewal conditions arrived as a list. No outside groups without a certificate of insurance and a named-insured endorsement. No unaccompanied public access. No polling site — the county asked in 2032 and the risk committee said no, politely, citing crowd control. The campus is the safest and most beautiful it has ever been, and on a Saturday in October there is nobody on it.

personas.name: Nadia, 17
personas.vignette: She runs the civics club and wanted to register seniors to vote on campus in November, which is not permitted, so she does it at the Kroger on Roswell Road with a folding table. It goes fine. What she cannot stop noticing is that the school taught her the vocabulary — quorum, canvass, precinct — in a building that will not host any of it, and that the first time she saw an adult vote she was nineteen and it was in a supermarket vestibule. She likes her school. She has stopped describing it as part of the community, because she has looked up what that word means.

personas.name: Mr. Halloran, 19 years in
personas.vignette: He used to run the Saturday robotics open house — neighbourhood kids, no fee, a hundred and forty people through the shop. It ended in 2031 when the certificate-of-insurance requirement made it impossible for unaffiliated families to attend. He understands every individual reason. He also knows that six of his best students over two decades first walked into that shop on a Saturday as somebody's cousin, and that the pipeline he is now asked to build through targeted outreach used to build itself by leaving a door open.

personas.name: Grace
personas.vignette: She is a litigator and she wrote part of the risk-committee memo, and she believes every word of it. Nuclear verdicts in her own practice have tripled; she has seen what a plaintiff does with an open-campus policy and an incident. She also drives past the school on Sundays and finds the emptiness genuinely upsetting in a way she cannot put in a memo, and she has noticed that the arguments she makes professionally have quietly become the arguments she makes about her own child's life.

personas.name: Dr. Osei, Head of School
personas.vignette: Her renewal is contingent on the access controls; the broker was explicit. She could self-insure the community-use exposure for roughly $400,000 a year in retained risk, which the board would approve if she asked, and she has drafted the ask twice. The obstacle is not money. It is that she cannot describe the benefit in the language the board minutes require — the return on an open Saturday door is a robotics student in 2041 and a neighbourhood that knows your name, and neither belongs in a risk register.

scenarios.tension: The school is telling the truth in both directions and the two truths do not fit. It really is where community happens — for the enrolled, the vetted, the insured. And the operational logic that makes it safe enough to keep doing that has closed it to everyone else, one defensible clause at a time, so the institution now sells belonging while functioning as the least publicly accessible building on its own street. Nobody chose this. Each condition was reasonable, each was priced, and the thing that was lost — porousness, the accidental cousin at the Saturday open house — never appeared on any renewal document because it has no premium and no claim number.
provocations: What did our campus host ten years ago that it does not host now, and what would it cost in retained risk to restore one of those things?
Can we write the value of open community access in language a board minute can hold — and if we cannot, is that a failure of the value or of our accounting?
If the county asked us to be a polling place tomorrow, who decides, on what criteria, and would we be willing to publish the answer?

scenarios.title: The Determination
scenarios.axis: CU 05 resolving toward liability as governor — documented determinations become the operative artefact — crossed with CU 02 resolving toward evidence that no longer supports the categories the record requires

based_on.title: Does institutional liability become the real governor of what schools may do?
based_on.pole: Liability as governor — what a school records, and when, decides what it may do; the determination is the legally operative act.

based_on.title: When the exam stops being verifiable, what becomes proof of learning?
based_on.pole: Dimensional evidence — the science says reading, attention and risk are continuous, so the thresholds the record demands are administrative fictions.

scenarios.premise: By 2035 the learning science is settled and inconvenient: reading, attention and executive function are continuous traits with no natural cut point, and Mount Vernon teaches accordingly — profile-matched instruction for every student, no separate track. But the legal architecture runs on determinations. Accommodations, funding, testing arrangements and the school's own defensibility all require a named, dated finding that a specific child does or does not meet a threshold. So the school makes determinations it does not scientifically believe in, and its support programme, which is genuinely excellent, runs on a different logic entirely.

personas.name: Priya, 15
personas.vignette: She reads at the 31st percentile on phonological decoding and the 78th on semantic comprehension, which her teachers use well — she gets exactly the instruction that profile implies. She is also, formally, Not Determined, because 31 sits above the line. Her friend Wes is at 27 and has a determination, and gets the same instruction Priya does, plus extra time on external exams. Priya has worked out that four percentile points, on one of two measures, is the whole difference. She has stopped mentioning it because it makes her sound like she is complaining about a friend.

personas.name: Mr. Adeyemi, 12 years in
personas.vignette: He writes two documents for every student now. The profile, which is true and useful and drives what he actually does on Monday. And the determination language, which uses a vocabulary of thresholds and deficits he was taught in 2029 was scientifically obsolete, because that is the language the accommodations file requires. He is fluent in both. What bothers him is that he is good at the second one — he can write a determination that gets a child what they need, and he knows that skill is a form of advocacy that has nothing to do with teaching.

personas.name: Tom
personas.vignette: He paid for the private evaluation, $4,200, because the school's own assessment put his daughter four points the wrong side of a line. The private one found a determination. He is not naive about what he bought and he does not feel good about it, and he would tell you plainly that a family without $4,200 has a child with the same brain and a different file. He has raised it at two parent evenings. Both times people agreed with him warmly and nothing happened, because nobody in the room controls the threshold.

personas.name: Dr. Yeh, Head of School
personas.vignette: She has a paper from her learning-support director arguing the school should stop making determinations it does not believe and fund all supports universally from its own budget. It is intellectually correct and it would cost $2.1M a year, forfeit external testing accommodations that only a determination unlocks, and expose the school to a claim from any family whose child was later diagnosed elsewhere and could show the school declined to assess. She has read it four times. She has not circulated it.

scenarios.tension: The school got the science right and cannot act on it, because the legal instrument that protects children requires a category the science says does not exist. Refusing to make determinations would be honest and would strip students of accommodations and the institution of its defence; making them sustains a threshold that everyone in the building knows is arbitrary and that wealth can purchase across. The record is not a description of the child. It is the child's legal standing, and it has quietly become the thing the school is really administering — while the actual teaching, which is good and evidence-based, happens alongside it in a language the file cannot hold.
provocations: Where do our own assessment thresholds sit, who set them, and can anyone here articulate the evidence for that specific cut point rather than a nearby one?
How many of our determinations were unlocked by a privately funded external evaluation, and what is that number's trend? Would we publish it?
If we fully funded supports without requiring a determination, what would it cost — and which of the barriers to doing so are legal, which financial, and which simply that nobody has costed it?

scenarios.title: The Consent Form
scenarios.axis: CU 02 resolving toward assessment that can no longer measure its own population — the instruments have been consented away or corrupted — crossed with CU 04 resolving toward consent-led legitimacy, where parents gate what the school is permitted to know

based_on.title: When the exam stops being verifiable, what becomes proof of learning?
based_on.pole: Unmeasurable population — the school can still assess individual work, but has lost the census-level instruments that told it who was struggling.

based_on.title: Is the binding constraint on AI in schools capability — or legitimacy?
based_on.pole: Consent-led — what a school may know about a child is set by a signature, and the signature is now opt-in.

scenarios.premise: By 2033 nothing is measured without permission. The 2026 consent rulings hardened through a decade of litigation until every instrument touching a child's inner life — wellbeing screeners, belonging surveys, advisory check-ins that log anything — requires an affirmative parental signature each year. Mount Vernon's return rate is 61%, which is excellent for the sector. The school is very good at helping the students it can see. It has stopped being able to say, at any given moment, how many it cannot.

personas.name: Josiah, 14
personas.vignette: His mother didn't return the form, the same way she doesn't return most forms — two jobs, not distrust. So he is not in the advisory data, not in the belonging index, not in the Tuesday flag list. He is fine, mostly. He had a hard November that nobody logged, and it passed on its own, and he is aware in a way he cannot articulate that if it had not passed on its own, the passing would also not have been noticed. He has never once thought of himself as invisible. He would say the school is good.

personas.name: Ms. Trujillo, 8 years in
personas.vignette: She has thirty-one students and consent for nineteen. The dashboard is genuinely useful for those nineteen. For the other twelve she is back to instinct, and she has become quietly excellent at it — she notices things now that she used to let the system notice. What unsettles her is that her instincts were trained on the students she can see, and the twelve are not a random twelve. They are, disproportionately, the families with the least time to read a form in April.

personas.name: Andrea
personas.vignette: She signs everything, reads it first, and thinks the consent regime is correct — she remembers what the old opt-out screeners collected and how casually it moved between systems. She also knows her daughter is in every dataset the school has, gets flagged early, gets the intervention. She has been on the parent council long enough to see the response-rate slide each autumn and to notice nobody says the obvious thing out loud: the families who protect their children by signing and the families who lose them by not signing are the same decision, made from different amounts of slack.

personas.name: Dr. Osei, Head of School
personas.vignette: Her defensible options are all forms of guessing. She can chase the 39% harder, which reads as pressure and lands on the busiest families. She can push everything into universal defaults that need no data — auto-enrol everyone into support, opt-out only — which works and costs a fortune. Or she can accept that her equity reporting now describes a self-selected population and footnote it honestly, which is the truthful choice and the one that looks worst in the annual report. She has been doing a version of the second and writing the third.

scenarios.tension: The consent regime is right. It was built because schools genuinely over-collected and moved children's inner lives around carelessly, and the families who fought for it were correct. It also produced a school that knows most about the children whose parents have time to be known, and is blind in exactly the direction its equity work is supposed to point. The mechanism protecting privacy and the mechanism producing invisibility are the same signature, and there is no version of the form that separates them — because a consent regime measures parental capacity to consent, and calls the result data.
provocations: What is our consent return rate, and how does it correlate with financial aid status? Have we ever run that correlation, and what would we do if it is what we expect?
Which of our supports could be redesigned as universal defaults requiring no individual data at all — and what would it cost to run them that way for everyone?
When we report on belonging or wellbeing to the board, do we state the response rate and who is missing from it? If not, what are we actually reporting?

scenarios.title: What We Knew
scenarios.axis: CU 05 resolving toward the campus as essential place — the school is where a child is genuinely known — crossed with CU 04 resolving toward liability as the binding constraint, where every act of knowing becomes a discoverable record

based_on.title: Does the physical campus become more essential — or a stranded asset?
based_on.pole: Essential place — the school's value is that it holds a continuous, human picture of a child that no other institution does.

based_on.title: Is the binding constraint on AI in schools capability — or legitimacy?
based_on.pole: Liability-gated — neither capability nor consent governs adoption; documented duty and discoverability do.

scenarios.premise: Mount Vernon's case for itself in 2034 is simple and true: nobody else knows your child. Not the tutoring platform, not the health system, not the county. Thirteen years of observations, screenings, genomic risk flags forwarded from paediatrics, advisor notes, the small recorded moment in Year 4 when someone wrote that Theo had gone quiet. It is the most complete portrait of a young person anywhere, and families choose the school for it. It is also, since the mandated-reporting rulings and the screening-negligence line of cases, the single largest discoverable archive the institution holds — and the school's own lawyers have started calling it, without irony, the file.

personas.name: Theo, 16
personas.vignette: He requested his record in the spring, which the 2031 access statute entitles him to, and read four hundred pages over a weekend. Most of it was kind. Someone in Year 4 wrote 'seems lonely at break, worth watching' and somebody did watch, and it helped. But he also learned he has carried a flagged variant since he was two weeks old and that eleven adults knew before he did, and there is a note from Year 7 about his mother that he wishes he had not read. He has not decided whether he is grateful. He thinks he probably is.

personas.name: Ms. Rowe, 6 years in
personas.vignette: She was trained to write down what she notices, and she does, and she has watched it save at least one student. But she now composes every entry twice — once as observation, once as it will read aloud in a deposition in 2041 — and the second draft is always flatter. She has caught herself not writing something because she wasn't sure enough to defend it, and the whole point of the early note is that you are not sure yet. She does not know who to raise this with. It sounds, said out loud, like she is asking permission to be careless.

personas.name: Renata
personas.vignette: She fought for the continuity of it — she is the reason the school integrated the health flags at all, after her older daughter fell through three systems that each held a third of the picture. She would do it again. What she did not anticipate was signing the annual consent this year and noticing there was no version of it that let her have the noticing without the archive, and that a school which knows everything about her son is, necessarily, a school that has written everything about her son down.

personas.name: Dr. Yeh, Head of School
personas.vignette: Counsel's advice is unambiguous and she cannot follow it. Retain less, write less, standardise the language, review before entry. Every measure reduces exposure and every measure degrades the thing families pay for. She has a retention schedule on her desk that would delete pastoral notes after six years. It would have deleted the Year 4 note about Theo. She has not signed it. She has not refused to sign it either, and the folder has been on the corner of the desk since March.

scenarios.tension: The school's deepest virtue and its gravest exposure turn out to be one artefact. Knowing a child means recording what you notice before you are certain, and an uncertain note is precisely what a plaintiff's counsel reads aloud in 2041 to establish that the institution knew. So the rational institutional response is to notice less formally, remember less durably, write more defensively — and every increment of that makes the school marginally safer and marginally less like the place families chose. There is no version of this that trades off cleanly, because the same sentence is the care and the evidence.
provocations: What is our retention schedule for pastoral observations — and can we articulate, in writing, why that number is right rather than merely defensible?
Do our teachers believe they can record an uncertain concern without it being used against them or the school? Have we ever asked them, and would we want the answer discoverable?
We are accumulating health and genomic data because integration serves students. Who at this school is accountable for the fact that the archive outlives the child's ability to consent to it?

scenarios.title: The Derivation
scenarios.axis: CU 01 resolving toward machines as a source of method — supplying techniques humans cannot invent but can learn and pass on — crossed with CU 02 resolving toward live defence, after the professions themselves normalised machine-written prose

based_on.title: Does routine AI use build human capability or quietly dissolve it?
based_on.pole: Machines as source of method — AI supplies techniques no human in the room derived, which humans then learn, use well, and transmit.

based_on.title: When the exam stops being verifiable, what becomes proof of learning?
based_on.pole: Live defence — writing is assumed machine-assisted everywhere, so proof moves to what a student can answer out loud, unaided, in a room.

scenarios.premise: By 2032 nobody pretends written work is unassisted; the research literature stopped pretending first, and schools followed. Mount Vernon assesses almost everything through defence: fifteen minutes, two examiners, no screen. It works. It is also the year the tenth-grade chemistry sequence adopted a separation protocol that came out of an optimisation run at a materials lab — faster and cleaner than the textbook method, and derived by no one. Students learn it, use it, teach it to the year below. The defence questions about it are answerable. The question of why it works is not, and the department has quietly stopped asking it.

personas.name: Amara, 16
personas.vignette: She defended the protocol on Thursday and did well — she could justify every step, predict what breaks if you change the temperature, explain the trade-off against the old method. Afterwards she asked Dr. Prashad why the second wash works and he said, honestly, that nobody knows, it just does, it fell out of the search. She has been turning that over since. She is not upset about it exactly. She has just noticed that she has never before learned something no person understood, and she cannot tell whether that makes her more capable or less.

personas.name: Dr. Prashad, 22 years in
personas.vignette: He can teach the protocol. He cannot derive it, and after four months of trying he has accepted he probably never will — the reasoning, if there is any, is not in a form a person holds. What unsettles him is how good the results are. His students are more competent than any cohort he has taught, on a method he does not understand, and he catches himself hoping a student will one day ask a question he cannot deflect, because that would mean the understanding still matters to someone besides him.

personas.name: Ellen
personas.vignette: She is a nurse and she is unbothered. Half of what she does at work rests on protocols nobody at the bedside derived either, and she has watched that save lives for twenty years. Her sister, an engineer, thinks the school is teaching cargo cult. They argued about it at dinner and neither could quite land the blow, because Ellen's version has outcomes on its side and her sister's has something harder to name — a claim about what school is supposed to be for that neither of them can make precise.

personas.name: Dr. Osei, Head of School
personas.vignette: Defence assessment has been the school's best decade of work and she is not going back. But she has started reading the protocol adoptions the way a lawyer reads a contract, because there is now a category of thing the school teaches that it cannot itself vouch for, and no policy governs how it enters the curriculum. A department head decides. She is drafting language and keeps deleting it, because every version either forbids something clearly good or permits everything.

scenarios.tension: Making assessment honest and making knowledge legible turn out to be different projects, and the first one succeeded. A student can now demonstrate real command of a method — apply it, predict its failures, teach it onward — while the chain of human understanding behind it is simply absent, and no defence question detects the difference, because competence and comprehension have come apart and only one of them is testable. Schools have always transmitted more than any individual teacher understood; what is new is that the surplus no longer sits in some other human's head. It sits nowhere.
provocations: Do we have a policy for adopting a method whose derivation no person can supply — and who currently makes that call, department by department, without one?

Our defence assessments test whether a student can use and justify a method. Should any of them test whether a student can reconstruct why it works — and what do we do when the answer is that nobody can?
If competence without comprehension produces better outcomes, what exactly is our argument for comprehension, and is it one we are prepared to make to a parent whose child is thriving?

scenarios.title: The Placement Rate
scenarios.axis: CU 04 resolving toward capability-led adoption — institutions embed AI structurally through accreditation and mandate — crossed with CU 03 resolving toward the market repricing the credential around measurable outcomes

based_on.title: Is the binding constraint on AI in schools capability — or legitimacy?
based_on.pole: Capability-led — accreditors and regulators embed AI and outcome measurement structurally, and adoption runs at the speed of policy rather than consent.

based_on.title: Does the academic credential hold its economic value, or does the market reprice it?
based_on.pole: Market reprices — schools are judged on what happens to graduates, and the metric that wins is continuous full-time attachment rather than prestige.

scenarios.premise: The accreditation reforms that began in 2026 finished arriving around 2031, and they brought a number with them. Every accredited school now reports a six-year Sustained Attachment Rate: the share of graduates in continuous full-time work or full-time study seventy-two months out. It was designed for colleges and flowed downhill within two cycles, because independent schools discovered families would rather see one honest number than a viewbook. Mount Vernon publishes 91.4%, third in the metro. The number is real. It is also, everyone quietly understands, the school's primary product now.

personas.name: Nina, 17
personas.vignette: She is good at exactly one thing — a decade of ceramics, hands that know what wet clay is about to do — and her advisor has been gently steering her toward supply-chain analytics since October, because the placement data on studio arts is what it is. Nobody has forbidden anything. Everyone has been kind. She has started describing ceramics as 'a hobby' in meetings, which is a word she never used before this year, and she noticed herself doing it and hasn't decided how she feels.

personas.name: Mr. Oyelaran, 14 years in
personas.vignette: His elective, Failure Lab, ran for nine years on the premise that students should build something ambitious and watch it not work. It was the course alumni wrote to him about. It was cut in the spring — not for cost, but because in the new curriculum audit every course maps to an attachment-outcome pathway, and a course whose stated purpose is productive failure could not be made to map. He was asked to propose a revised version. He is finding that he cannot write the paperwork without lying.

personas.name: Dana
personas.vignette: She chose Mount Vernon over two cheaper schools on the strength of 91.4% and she would do it again. Her son is thriving, employed at twenty-three, insured. What she cannot shake is a conversation at a barbecue where three parents compared attachment rates the way their own parents compared college acceptances, and she heard herself join in fluently, and realised she could no longer describe what she wanted for her son in any language other than his employment status at thirty.

personas.name: Dr. Osei, Head of School
personas.vignette: She can move the number four ways: counsel students toward high-attachment fields, cut courses that don't map, admit slightly differently, or support graduates harder after they leave. Three are cheap and one is expensive. The board has never instructed her to do the cheap ones and she has done two of them anyway, incrementally, over four years, each decision defensible on its own. She keeps a list of what the school stopped offering. She has not shown it to anyone.

scenarios.tension: Accountability finally arrived in a form nobody could game with marketing, and it worked — the number is honest, families can compare schools, and graduates really are more secure. But a metric doesn't just measure a school; it slowly becomes the school, and this one measures employment continuity, which is a real good and a narrow one. Nothing was banned. No villain decided ceramics didn't matter. A thousand individually defensible choices simply drifted toward what the number rewards, and the things that made the place worth attending were the things the number could not see.
provocations: If an outcome metric like this became standard, what would we refuse to optimise — and could we write that refusal down before we are under pressure, rather than after?
Which of our current offerings would fail a curriculum audit that required every course to map to a measurable graduate outcome? Are we willing to defend them on other grounds, in public?

We already track college matriculation. In what ways is that number already shaping our counselling in the direction this scenario describes, and who at this school is authorised to name that out loud?

scenarios.title: The Waiting Room
scenarios.axis: CU 01 resolving toward conditional amplification — AI helps only those already disposed to ask — crossed with CU 05 resolving toward the campus as essential third place

based_on.title: Does routine AI use build human capability or quietly dissolve it?
based_on.pole: Conditional amplification — the tool multiplies whatever disposition a student already brings, and does almost nothing for those who never ask it a real question.

based_on.title: Does the physical campus become more essential — or a stranded asset?
based_on.pole: Essential third place — the scarce good turns out to be an adult who notices, and that cannot be delivered remotely.

scenarios.premise: By 2034 the AI tutor question is settled and the answer is uncomfortable: it works, but only for students who already ask questions. A decade of trials converged on the same finding — the tool multiplies disposition rather than supplying it, and the gap between students who interrogate a wrong answer and those who click past it has widened into the primary axis of inequality. Schools responded by hiring back the thing software cannot do: adults who notice. Mount Vernon's most oversubscribed offering is no longer a course. It is a room, staffed all day, where a student can sit next to a person and be asked what they are stuck on.

personas.name: Dev, 15
personas.vignette: He has had an AI tutor since he was six and it has taught him almost nothing, because he has never once typed what he actually doesn't understand. He types what will make the session end. In the Waiting Room on Tuesday, Ms. Alvarez sat down, looked at his screen for eleven seconds and said 'you don't know what a variable is, do you' — and he cried, which was humiliating, and then it was the best week of school he'd had. There are forty-one names on the Waiting Room list. He got in because his advisor pushed.

personas.name: Ms. Alvarez, 9 years in
personas.vignette: She teaches two sections now instead of five; the rest of her load is Waiting Room hours. It is the most skilled work she has ever done and the least legible — no unit plan, no rubric, nothing to show at an accreditation visit except students who got unstuck. She can hold about nine kids in her head with real fidelity. The school has assigned her twenty-six. She has started quietly triaging toward the ones who will respond fastest, and she knows exactly what that does to the ones who won't, and she does it anyway.

personas.name: Marcus
personas.vignette: He pays $71,000 and he has done the arithmetic: the AI does the instruction, so what he is buying is Ms. Alvarez's attention, and there is provably not enough of it. He asked at the parent forum how Waiting Room access is allocated. The answer was 'advisor referral,' which he understood immediately to mean that the parents who ask get more. He asked anyway. He is not proud of this and he would do it again tomorrow.

personas.name: Dr. Yeh, Head of School
personas.vignette: Her enrollment is healthy and her county's school-age population fell nine percent in six years — the two facts coexist because families are consolidating into fewer, better-staffed schools, and she is one of them. She is absorbing students from three closures. Every marginal student improves the budget and dilutes the one thing families are actually buying. There is a number at which the Waiting Room stops working and becomes a queue, and nobody at the board table wants to be the person who names it out loud.

scenarios.tension: The decade's most hopeful finding and its most troubling one are the same finding. AI turned out not to replace teachers; it revealed which part of teaching was irreplaceable, and that part is human attention — which does not scale, cannot be bought in bulk, and is now the explicit product of an expensive school. Every previous inequality in education was at least partly about access to materials, and materials got cheap. This one is about access to a person who notices you, and that has gotten more expensive every year. A school that responds well to this becomes very good and very exclusive at the same time, by the same mechanism, and cannot separate the two.
provocations: What is our actual student-to-noticing-adult ratio, as opposed to our student-teacher ratio — and would we publish it?
If attention is the scarce good we sell, what is our written rule for allocating it, and does that rule survive a parent reading it?
As neighbouring schools contract and we absorb their students, at what enrollment number does our core value proposition break? Who is authorised to say we have reached it?

scenarios.title: The Defense
scenarios.axis: CU 02 resolving toward performance redesign × CU 03 resolving toward the market repricing the credential

based_on.title: When the exam stops being verifiable, what becomes proof of learning?
based_on.pole: Performance redesign — verification moves from the artifact to the person in the room.

based_on.title: Does the academic credential hold its economic value, or does the market reprice it?
based_on.pole: Market reprices — demonstrated capability displaces the transcript at the point of entry.

scenarios.premise: By 2033 the transcript is a formality. Mount Vernon's diploma is awarded on a portfolio defense: ninety minutes before a panel of two faculty and two outside practitioners, defending a body of work built over eighteen months. Employers across the metro hire directly off defense recordings. The SAT still exists. Almost nobody submits one.

personas.name: Maya, 17
personas.vignette: Her defense is in four days and it is good — a water-quality sensor network she built with the county, eleven months of real deployment data, two failures she can explain better than the successes. She is not worried about the work. She is worried that Tobias's panel includes his mother's former colleague, and that Ren's includes someone his family had to dinner in March. Nobody broke a rule. Maya's mother drives a school bus. When the exam existed, Maya knew exactly what she was being measured against, and it was the same thing everyone else was measured against. She misses that and feels ridiculous for missing it.

personas.name: Dan, 11 years in
personas.vignette: He does not grade anymore. He coaches for eighteen months and then formally recuses himself from the panel, which is the best change to his working life in a decade — no more arguing about a B+. But there is a student in his section with nothing defensible, and Dan has run out of things to say to him. The old answer was study harder; there was a test, and effort had somewhere to go. Now the students who flounder are the ones without a project worth ninety minutes, and Dan cannot assign someone a compelling life. The redesign raised the ceiling and quietly removed the floor.

personas.name: Priya
personas.vignette: Fifty-eight thousand a year, from sixth grade, for a college-preparatory education. Her daughter was offered a job at seventeen by a panelist and is deferring college — possibly indefinitely. Priya has told exactly three people. She is proud in a way she cannot say cleanly, because she cannot work out whether the school delivered spectacularly on something she never asked for, or failed completely at the one thing she actually bought. Her own parents will ask about college at Thanksgiving. She has not decided what to say.

personas.name: Dr. Ellis, Head of School
personas.vignette: Inquiries are up thirty percent and the waitlist is real for the first time since 2019. Three corporate partners have asked, politely and separately, whether they might have standing seats on defense panels. Each would be a genuine gift to students. Together they would make the school something closer to a talent pipeline with a curriculum attached. She has no policy governing who sits on a panel, because for a hundred years the answer was nobody — a proctor handed out a test. She has to write that policy this year, and whatever she writes will be quoted back to her for a decade.

scenarios.tension: The future in which assessment finally became authentic is also the one in which the school's gatekeeping power grew rather than dissolved. A standardized test is a crude instrument, but it is legible to a family with no connections — and legibility, it turns out, was doing equity work that nobody credited it for. Replacing it with human judgment in a room full of adults does not remove bias; it relocates bias somewhere harder to audit and impossible to appeal.
provocations: If we move to defense-style assessment, what is our written policy on who may sit on a panel — and who may not?
What is the floor? What does a student get to be measured against when they have not produced anything remarkable?
If an employer hires our seventeen-year-old, have we succeeded or failed at the thing families are paying for?

challenger.title: Where does the student end and the equipment begin?
challenger.why: The line between a person and their apparatus is dissolving from four directions at once, and schools have no rule that survives any of them. Display glasses with live captioning now ship at $499 in 40 countries, waveguide AR shipments are up 600%, and the same object is an accommodation, a translation aid and an undetectable exam device. Consumer BCI has been cleared outside the medical pathway, non-invasive decoding can type from brain activity, and Vermont has legislated neural rights while student neural data sits in no policy anywhere. AI companions are close enough to persons that product updates trigger measurable grief in adolescents, and students have begun formally contesting LLM classifications of their own speech. Every school policy in this territory — devices, integrity, accessibility, privacy, even discipline — assumes a clean boundary at the skin, and that assumption is now false in cheap consumer hardware rather than in theory.
challenger.why_not_yet: Day four, neither trigger fired, and the dedicated weak-signal hunt again returned an honest null on both — worth recording, because two consecutive null results from targeted searching is itself information. What did surface is the regulatory shadow of trigger (b): IEEE P7700, an active standards project on responsible neurotechnology chaired by neuroethicist Laura Cabrera, was stood up precisely because neurodevices are moving from therapeutic users to consumers, and its working group explicitly names devices marketed to students to improve attention span. A numbered standard is the thing a parent points at; none exists yet. Adjacent and sharper: an IETF Internet-Draft on age-verification architecture states that facial age estimation is 'notoriously unreliable... especially for teenagers'. That is the same structure as the boundary question — a machine reading a body to decide what a student may do — arriving through age assurance rather than through assessment. On trigger (a), the accommodation-versus-integrity collision still has no case, complaint, examining-board decision or published school policy anywhere; the hunt confirms it is structurally inevitable and simply unlitigated. RETIREMENT CONDITION stands: if neither trigger has fired and no displacement case is made by 21 September, retire cu-boundary to a watch list and name a better-grounded successor — the age-assurance framing is currently the most likely successor.
